nameStory: The "leafy brain" name captures this fungus's wild appearance perfectly — it looks like a wrinkled brain made of thin, leaf-like layers. The brownish, folded surface with its convoluted ridges and valleys really does resemble brain tissue, but flattened into delicate, overlapping sheets like autumn leaves.
description: Leafy brain is a jelly fungus that creates some of nature's most unusual art on dead conifer branches. This parasitic fungus produces brownish, gelatinous fruit bodies that emerge as thin, leaf-like lobes with a distinctly brain-like, wrinkled surface. The entire mass can range from a few inches to over a foot across, looking like someone draped wet, translucent leather over a tree branch. It's actually a parasite that feeds on another fungus growing in the dead wood.

idTips.label: Jelly-like texture
idTips.description: Touch reveals a firm but bouncy, gelatinous feel — like thick Jell-O or wet rubber that springs back when pressed

idTips.label: Brownish color
idTips.description: Ranges from light tan to dark chocolate brown, often with a slightly translucent quality that lets light filter through

idTips.label: Leafy, brain-like form
idTips.description: Grows in thin, overlapping lobes with deeply wrinkled, convoluted surfaces that feel like wet chamois leather

idTips.label: Host location
idTips.description: Always found on dead or dying conifer branches, never on living trees or hardwood species

idTips.label: Wet weather appearance
idTips.description: Becomes more prominent and translucent when moist, shrinking to dark, crusty patches during dry spells

habitat: Look for leafy brain on dead and dying branches of conifers throughout New England's forests, particularly on pine, spruce, and fir trees. It favors recently fallen branches or dead limbs still attached to trees, thriving in the moist conditions of mixed and coniferous woodlands. You'll often spot it in areas with good air circulation but protection from direct sun.

seasonality.spring: Fresh fruit bodies begin emerging as temperatures warm and spring rains provide moisture. Look for small, brownish patches starting to develop their characteristic wrinkled texture.
seasonality.summer: Not typically active during hot, dry summer months unless in consistently moist areas. Existing fruit bodies may shrivel to dark, crusty remnants.
seasonality.fall: Peak season for finding well-developed specimens as cool, wet weather returns. Fruit bodies reach full size and display their most dramatic leafy, brain-like appearance.
seasonality.winter: Persists through mild winter weather, becoming more gelatinous during warm spells and freezing solid during cold snaps, then reviving when temperatures rise.

funFact: This fungus is actually a parasite of another parasite — it doesn't directly attack the dead wood, but instead feeds on a different fungus that's already decomposing the branch, making it a "hyperparasite" that lives off another decomposer!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other jelly fungi like amber jelly or witch's butter, but those species are typically more blob-like rather than thin and leafy. Remember: if it looks like wet brain tissue made of leaves and it's on a conifer branch, you've found leafy brain.
contextualKnowledge: This species was recently moved from the genus Tremella to Phaeotremella based on DNA studies, so you may still see it listed as Tremella foliacea in older field guides. The name changes reflect scientists' better understanding of fungal relationships, but the fungus itself hasn't changed at all.
compareHints: Leafy brain differs from its close relatives by its distinctly leaf-like, thin lobes rather than the more massive, brain-like folds of Phaeotremella frondosa. While both species have that characteristic jelly texture, leafy brain's fruit bodies are much more delicate and translucent, creating overlapping sheets rather than thick, bulbous masses.
